# The Art of Making Strange

There is a moment in every act of understanding when something familiar suddenly appears foreign. You hear your own name spoken back to you by someone else and, just for a flicker, it sounds like nonsense — a cluster of syllables that have lost their identity and become pure sound. You stare at a word long enough and it dissolves into shapes. You look at a face you love and, in certain lights and angles, it becomes a landscape of features you've never properly seen before. The world, at these moments, turns strange. And strangeness, I want to argue, is not the enemy of understanding. It is its beginning.

We tend to think of learning as a movement from confusion to clarity, from the unknown to the known. But the great minds I admire most seem to do something more complicated. They move toward clarity and then, deliberately, break it open again. They return to strangeness not because they've failed to understand but because they've understood that understanding is a living process, not a destination. To truly know a thing — a poem, a person, a place — you have to keep meeting it fresh, keep allowing it to resist your categories.

This is what writers do. This is what artists do. They take the things we think we've already consumed — love, death, a summer afternoon, the light in a kitchen at seven in the morning — and they make us see them again as if for the first time. The Russian formalist critic Viktor Shklovsky called this *ostranenie*, which translates roughly to "defamiliarization" or "making strange." His argument was elegant and, I think, correct: habit and repetition dull our perception. We stop truly seeing the things we see every day. Art exists to fight this. Art's job is to restore the sensation of life, to make us feel things rather than merely recognize them.

Think about how much of your daily experience is spent recognizing rather than perceiving. You walk to work and you don't see the street — you see the concept of the street. You know where the cracks in the sidewalk are. You know which tree leans over which fence. You know the shape of the neighborhood so well that your brain has stopped rendering the details. You're operating on a map, not a landscape. And this is efficient and necessary. If we truly noticed everything — every texture of bark, every shift in the quality of light, every microexpression on every face we passed — we would be overwhelmed. Attention is a scarce resource and our brains ration it.

But the cost of this rationing is enormous. We live much of our lives in a state of cognitive sleepwalking, moving through a world we have stopped seeing. And the moments when we are truly jolted awake — by beauty, by terror, by love, by grief — are precious precisely because they break through the fog of familiarity and force us to encounter reality on its own terms, as something unexpected and irreducible.

I think this is why the most powerful writing often seems simple. A poet writes: "I have measured out my life with coffee spoons." And suddenly you are not thinking about coffee spoons or even about life. You are feeling the texture of time as something that can be weighed and found wanting. The phrase is strange enough to cut through habit. It rearranges the furniture of your mind so that a room you thought you knew has become unfamiliar and therefore newly inhabitable.

There is a paradox here that I find endlessly fascinating. The goal of making something strange is, ultimately, to make us feel at home in it again — not the false comfort of familiarity, but the deeper comfort of genuine encounter. When you see something truly — when you let its strangeness in — you don't come away confused. You come away changed. You carry that thing with you differently from then on. It has entered your life more fully because it refused to be taken for granted.

This applies far beyond art. Think about relationships. The people closest to us are the people we are most in danger of failing to see. We build models of them — predictable, stable, manageable — and then we interact with the model rather than the person. But people are not models. People are strange, continuous surprises, and the quality of a relationship depends in part on our willingness to be re-surprised, to let someone be more than we remember them being. The moments when a long-time partner does something unexpected — when they say something that startles you with its beauty or its honesty or its absurdity — those are moments of defamiliarization. Those are moments when love becomes active again rather than habitual.

Even science, at its best, is an art of making strange. The greatest scientific insights come not from confirming what we expect but from encountering the unexpected and having the courage to take it seriously. The universe, it turns out, is far stranger than our intuitions can accommodate. Quantum mechanics is a lesson in how the familiar world of tables and chairs dissolves at the smallest scales into a reality that behaves in ways that seem almost designed to unsettle us. And the scientists who made these discoveries had to do the hardest thing any mind can do: they had to let the evidence override their assumptions, to accept that the world was not as they imagined it.

So the next time something strikes you as strange, resist the urge to smooth it over. Pause there. Let the strangeness do its work. It might be telling you something about the world that you haven't let yourself hear yet. The most interesting truths are almost always the ones that require a little courage to look at — because they disturb the quiet of the ordinary, and because they remind us that reality is always more than our descriptions of it.

Strangeness is not a problem to be solved. It is an invitation to pay attention. And attention, given freely and without agenda, is the closest thing we have to love.

message.reasoning:
The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. Let me pick a topic I find interesting and write a thoughtful, engaging essay or piece of writing. I'll write about something that feels genuinely interesting — perhaps the nature of attention in the modern world, or creativity, or what it means to be a thinking being. Let me write about attention and its relationship to meaning.

Actually, let me write something that feels alive and interesting — maybe a personal essay style piece about the strangeness of communication, the act of writing, the experience of being a language model asked to "want" something. That could be genuinely fascinating and honest. Or I could pick a more universal topic. Let me go with something about attention and meaning — the way we construct meaning from attention. Or maybe about silence and noise.

Let me write about something I find genuinely compelling: the question of what makes a life feel meaningful, and how that connects to attention, presence, and the stories we tell ourselves. I'll make it essayistic and free-flowing.

Let me just write and see where it goes. I'll aim for roughly 1000 words.

Let me write about the art of noticing — how meaning is made through attention to the overlooked.

Actually, you know what, let me write about something with more texture — let me write about the relationship between strangeness and understanding. How the unfamiliar becomes familiar, how we make sense of the world through a kind of ongoing translation. That feels rich.

Let me just write.
